title: Zero-density estimates
summary: $N(\sigma, T)$ counts zeros with real part at least $\sigma$ and height at most $T$. Density theorems show $N(\sigma,T) \ll T^{A(1-\sigma)+\varepsilon}$: zeros off the line, if any, are rare.
why: Density hypotheses give primes in short intervals almost as well as RH would.
references: Titchmarsh, The Theory of the Riemann Zeta-Function

title: Lindelöf hypothesis and subconvexity
summary: Lindelöf (1908) conjectured $\zeta(\tfrac12+it) \ll |t|^{\varepsilon}$. The functional equation and convexity give exponent $\tfrac14$; any improvement is called subconvexity.
why: Implied by RH, and itself enough for many applications.
references: Titchmarsh, The Theory of the Riemann Zeta-Function

title: Pair correlation and random matrices
summary: Montgomery (1973) studied spacings between zeros and conjectured their pair correlation is $1 - \left(\frac{\sin \pi u}{\pi u}\right)^2$. Dyson recognised this as the eigenvalue statistics of large random Hermitian matrices.
why: Zeros behave like energy levels of a chaotic quantum system, a hint toward the Hilbert–Pólya idea.

prerequisites.title: Nontrivial zeros and the Riemann–von Mangoldt formula

timeline.title: Pair correlation of zeros
timeline.text: His conjectured spacing law matched random matrix statistics, as Freeman Dyson pointed out.

timeline.title: Moments from random matrices
timeline.text: Predicted the moments of $\zeta$ on the critical line from random matrix theory.

title: Diophantine approximation and irrationality
summary: How well can a real number be approximated by $p/q$? Dirichlet gives $|\alpha - p/q| < 1/q^2$ infinitely often; Roth (1955) shows algebraic irrationals cannot do much better. Irrationality proofs (Apéry's $\zeta(3)$) are quantitative statements of this kind.
key_statements: \Big|\alpha-\frac pq\Big| < \frac{1}{q^{2+\varepsilon}} \ \text{has finitely many solutions for algebraic } \alpha \ \text{(Roth)}
why: Transcendence, the abc conjecture and the irrationality of zeta values all reduce to how small a linear form in numbers can be.
references: Hardy & Wright, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers

timeline.title: Roth's approximation theorem
timeline.text: Algebraic irrationals have approximation exponent exactly $2$; Fields Medal 1958.

title: Smooth, powerful and squarefree numbers
summary: $n$ is $y$-smooth if all its prime factors are $\le y$, powerful if $p\mid n \Rightarrow p^2 \mid n$, squarefree if no $p^2$ divides it. Their counts are governed by Dickman's function, $\zeta(3/2)/\zeta(3)\cdot\sqrt x$ and $6x/\pi^2$.
why: Smooth numbers are the engine of the fastest factoring algorithms; powerful numbers are where the abc conjecture bites.
references: Tenenbaum, Introduction to Analytic and Probabilistic Number Theory
Crandall & Pomerance, Prime Numbers: A Computational Perspective

prerequisites.title: Primes and the fundamental theorem of arithmetic

title: Primes in sequences and gaps
summary: Which sequences contain infinitely many primes, how large gaps between consecutive primes can be, and how often primes fall in short intervals. Most such questions are open; sieves and the circle method give the partial results.
why: Large gaps are built by covering an interval with residue classes, so this topic shares a toolkit with covering systems.
references: Guy, Unsolved Problems in Number Theory

timeline.title: The primes contain arbitrarily long progressions
timeline.text: A relative Szemerédi theorem applied to a pseudorandom majorant of the primes.

title: Probabilistic number theory
summary: Arithmetic functions behave like sums of independent random variables. Erdős–Kac: $\omega(n)$, the number of prime factors, is normally distributed with mean and variance $\log\log n$.
why: It turned heuristics such as Cramér's model of the primes into theorems where it could, and tells you what to expect where it cannot.
references: Tenenbaum, Introduction to Analytic and Probabilistic Number Theory

prerequisites.title: The law of large numbers and the central limit theorem

timeline.title: The Erdős–Kac theorem
timeline.text: $\omega(n)$ is asymptotically normal with mean and variance $\log\log n$.
